name: Asaiah
title: King's Servant in the Time of Josiah
summary: Asaiah was one of King Josiah's trusted officials with the official title "the king's servant" (Hebrew: eved ha-melekh). When the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law in the temple during restoration work around 622 BC, Asaiah was appointed as a member of a high-ranking delegation to consult the prophetess Huldah for God's guidance regarding the book's content and its consequences for the people. The delegation included, among others, the high priest Hilkiah, the scribe Shaphan, Ahikam, and the court official Akbor. Huldah's prophetic message proclaimed coming judgment on Jerusalem because of the people's apostasy, but promised that King Josiah personally would be spared from experiencing the destruction because he had humbled himself. This event led to one of the most extensive religious reforms in Judah's history, with covenant renewal and cleansing from idolatry. Asaiah's name (Hebrew: עֲשָׂיָה) means "Yahweh has acted" — a theophoric name that was widespread in ancient Israel.

keyEvents.title: The Book of the Law Found in the Temple
keyEvents.description: During the temple restoration, the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law. When its contents were read to King Josiah, he reacted with deep grief and tore his clothes in despair over how the people had broken God's commands. He then ordered a delegation to seek the Lord's will.

keyEvents.title: Sent to the Prophetess Huldah
keyEvents.description: Asaiah was sent as part of a high-ranking delegation to the prophetess Huldah to consult on the contents of the discovered Book of the Law. The delegation consisted of the high priest Hilkiah, the scribe Shaphan, Shaphan's son Ahikam, Achbor (son of Micaiah according to Chronicles), and Asaiah himself.

keyEvents.title: Huldah's Prophecy of Judgment and Mercy
keyEvents.description: The prophetess Huldah gave the delegation a two-part message from the Lord: God would bring disaster upon Jerusalem and its inhabitants because of long-standing apostasy and idolatry, but King Josiah himself would be spared from seeing the great destruction because he had humbled himself and shown repentance.

keyEvents.title: The Message Leads to Covenant Renewal and Reformation
keyEvents.description: After the delegation, with Asaiah among its members, brought Huldah's prophetic message back to the king, Josiah gathered all the people in the temple and made a solemn covenant to follow the Lord's commands. This initiated an extensive religious reformation involving the removal of idolatry throughout Judah.

versions.summary: Asaiah was a servant of King Josiah of Judah who was sent along with others to consult the prophetess Huldah regarding the Book of the Law found in the temple. He played a role in the religious reformation during Josiah's reign. His name means 'the Lord has done' and he is mentioned in connection with the rediscovery of the Mosaic Law.
versions.title: Levite in the Time of King Josiah
versions.reason: [minor] The title calls Asaiah a 'Levite', but there is no evidence in the biblical text that he was a Levite. In 2 Kings 22:12 and 2 Chronicles 34:20, he is referred to as 'the king's servant' (Hebrew eved ha-melekh). There is another Asaiah who is a Levite (1 Chronicles 6:30). The title should be corrected.; [major] The summary refers to him as 'a servant of King Josiah', which is correct, but it contains an inaccuracy regarding the meaning of his name. 'Asaiah' (Hebrew עֲשָׂיָה) more precisely means 'the Lord has done/created' or 'Yahweh has acted'. Furthermore, it should be clarified that he was 'the king's servant' (a possible official title), not just generally 'a servant'.; [major] The role 'leader' is imprecise. Asaiah is described in the biblical text as 'the king's servant' (eved ha-melekh), which was likely an official position at the court. 'Royal advisor' or 'the king's servant' would be more precise than simply 'leader'.; [minor] In 2 Chronicles 34:14-18, verses 19-20 might need to be included to cover the entire sequence until the delegation is sent. Otherwise, the references are reasonable.; [minor] In 2 Kings 22:12, Asaiah is specifically mentioned as 'Asaiah, the king's servant'. Verse 12 is already included in the previous event as well, creating an overlap. Consider distinguishing more clearly between the events.; [minor] It is somewhat speculative to say that Asaiah was directly involved in the reform that followed. The Bible only mentions that the delegation brought the message back. It should be made clearer that Asaiah's role was primarily as part of the delegation, not as a reformer.; [major] There are no footnotes about interesting historical, archaeological, linguistic, or theological details. The title 'eved ha-melekh' (the king's servant) is a well-known term from both the biblical text and archaeological finds (seals/bullae). Footnotes should be added.

versions.summary: Asaiah was one of King Josiah's trusted men, with the official title "the king's servant" (Hebrew: eved ha-melekh). When the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law in the temple during restoration work, Asaiah was sent as part of a delegation to the prophetess Huldah to seek counsel about the book's content and its meaning for the people. Huldah's prophetic message concerning coming judgment on Jerusalem, yet mercy for Josiah personally, was brought back by the delegation and led to a widespread religious reform. Asaiah's name (Hebrew: עֲשָׂיָה) means "Yahweh has acted" and reflects a theophory that was common in ancient Israel.
versions.title: King's Servant in the Time of Josiah
versions.reason: [major] In 2 Chronicles 34, Asaiah is not specifically mentioned in verses 14-19. Asaiah (called Hilkiah in 2 Kings and similarly in 2 Chronicles) is first mentioned in connection with the delegation in verse 20. Verses 14-19 concern the finding of the book and its reading before the king, but Asaiah is not named here. It may still be included as context, but it should be clarified that these are background verses.; [minor] The last keyEvent stating that the delegation's report leads to reformation is relevant context, but Asaiah is not explicitly mentioned in these verses (2 Kings 23:1-3, 2 Chronicles 34:29-33). It may be acceptable to retain it as a contextual event, but the description should make clear that Asaiah's direct role here is assumed, not explicitly described.; [minor] The summary is good and informative. A small improvement could be to mention that Asaiah is also called 'Asaiah, the king's servant' in the parallel text of 2 Chronicles 34:20, to clarify the source basis.; [minor] The footnotes are good and relevant. An additional footnote could note the parallel between 2 Kings 22 and 2 Chronicles 34, and that the name forms vary somewhat between the two texts (in some translations he is called Asaiah or Abijah).

versions.title: King's Servant in the Time of Josiah
versions.reason: [minor] The last keyEvent (covenant renewal and reformation) primarily concerns Josiah's actions after the delegation returned. Asaiah's direct role in this event is not explicitly mentioned in the text. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to include it as a contextual outcome, but the description could have made clearer that Asaiah's role here is implicit as part of the delegation that delivered the message.; [minor] The phrasing "laid in his grave in peace" in Huldah's prophecy to Josiah is somewhat theologically disputed, since Josiah actually died in battle at Megiddo (2 Kgs 23:29). The prophecy is usually understood to mean that he would not experience the final destruction of Jerusalem. The summary gives an accurate rendering of the prophecy as it stands, but this could have been nuanced.; [minor] The roles "envoy" and "delegation member" largely overlap. It might have sufficed to use just one of these, or alternatively replaced "delegation member" with "official" to reflect his formal position.

footnotes.text: The title 'king's servant' (Hebrew: eved ha-melekh) was likely an official court position at the Judean royal court, not merely a general description. Several archaeological finds of seals (bullae) from the Iron Age bear this title along with personal names, confirming that it was a formal role in the king's administration.

The name Asaiah (Hebrew: עֲשָׂיָה, Asayah) is composed of the verb 'asah' (to do/act) and the shortened divine name form '-yah' (Yahweh). The name therefore means 'Yahweh has acted' or 'the Lord has done'. The name is theophoric, meaning it carries a reference to God, expressing gratitude for divine intervention.

The discovery of the Book of the Law in the temple during Josiah's reign (around 622 BC) is regarded by many scholars as a decisive moment in Israel's religious history. Many identify the found scroll with an early form of Deuteronomy, and the event triggered the so-called Deuteronomic reformation.

The prophetess Huldah is one of very few female prophets mentioned in the Old Testament. The fact that the king's delegation was sent to her rather than to contemporary male prophets like Jeremiah suggests she held high esteem and authority in Jerusalem at that time.

Asaiah is mentioned in 2 Kings 22:12, 14 and in 2 Chronicles 34:20. In Kings he is described as 'the king's servant', while Chronicles uses a similar title. The two parallel accounts complement each other and provide a combined picture of the delegation's composition and mission to the prophetess Huldah.

In rabbinic tradition, the oracle of the prophetess Huldah is attributed great significance, and the Talmud (Megillah 14b) counts her among the seven female prophets in Israel. The fact that Josiah sent his delegation to her—and not to Jeremiah—has given rise to various rabbinic interpretations, including the suggestion that women would likely show more mercy in delivering the message.
